## Late antiquity
### Byzantine period
In the Siege of Jerusalem of 614, after 21 days of relentless siege warfare, Jerusalem was captured. Byzantine chronicles relate that the Sassanids and Jews slaughtered tens of thousands of Christians in the city, many at the Mamilla Pool,[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Jerusalem#cite_note-43)[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Jerusalem#cite_note-44) and destroyed their monuments and churches, including the Church of the Holy Sepulchre. This episode has been the subject of much debate between historians.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Jerusalem#cite_note-45) Following the conquest, Jewish leaders briefly governed or held key roles in Jerusalem under Sassanid suzerainty (614–617 CE).[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Jerusalem#cite_note-46) In 617 AD, the Sassanid Empire reversed course and removed the Jewish control of the city. Jerusalem then stayed in Sassanid hands until the Byzantine emperor Heraclius reconquered it in 629.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Jerusalem#cite_note-47)

## Medieval period
### Early Muslim period
#### Rashidun, Umayyad and Abbasid Caliphates
Map of Jerusalem as it appeared in the years 958–1052, according to Arabgeographers such as al-Muqaddasi
The Hereford_Mapa Mundi_, depicting Jerusalem at the centre of the world
Jerusalem was one of the ArabCaliphate's first conquests in 638 CE; according to Arab historians of the time, the Rashidun Caliph Umar ibn al-Khattab personally went to the city to receive its submission, cleaning out and praying at the Temple Mount in the process. Umar ibn al-Khattab allowed the Jews back into the city and freedom to live and worship after almost three centuries of banishment by the Romans and Byzantines.

## Medieval period
### Early Muslim period
#### Rashidun, Umayyad and Abbasid Caliphates
Under the early centuries of Muslim rule, especially during the Umayyad (650–750) dynasty, the city prospered. Around 691–692 CE, the Dome of the Rock was built on the Temple Mount. Rather than a mosque, it is a shrine that enshrines the Foundation Stone. The Al-Aqsa Mosque was also built under Umayyad rule during the late 7th or early 8th century on the southern end of the compound, and was associated with a place of the same name mentioned in the Quran as a place visited by Muhammad during his [Night Journey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isra'_and_Mi'raj "Isra' and Mi'raj"). Jerusalem is not mentioned by any of its names in the Quran, and the Qur'an does not mention the exact location of Al-Aqsa Mosque.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Jerusalem#cite_note-Khatib-48)[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Jerusalem#cite_note-:9-49) Some scholars contend that the connection between the Al-Aqsa Mosque referenced in the Quran and the Temple Mount in Jerusalem is the result of an Umayyad political agenda that aimed to rival the prestige of the Mecca sanctuary, which was then ruled by their enemy, Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Jerusalem#cite_note-:8-50)[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Jerusalem#cite_note-51)
The Abbasid period (750–969) is the least documented of the early Muslim period in general. The Temple Mount area was the center of known building activity, with structures damaged in earthquakes being repaired.

## Medieval period
### Early Muslim period
#### Rashidun, Umayyad and Abbasid Caliphates
Geographers Ibn Hawqal and al-Istakhri (10th century) describe Jerusalem as "the most fertile province of Palestine",_[citation needed_] while its native son, the geographer al-Muqaddasi (born 946) devoted many pages to its praises in his most famous work, _The Best Divisions in the Knowledge of the Climes_. Under Muslim rule Jerusalem did not achieve the political or cultural status enjoyed by the capitals Damascus, Baghdad, Cairo etc. Al-Muqaddasi derives his name from the Arabic name for Jerusalem, _Bayt al-Muqaddas_, which is linguistically equivalent to the Hebrew _Beit Ha-Mikdash_, the Holy House.

## Medieval period
### Early Muslim period
#### Fatimid period
The early Arab period was also one of religious tolerance._[citation needed_] However, in the early 11th century, the Egyptian Fatimid CaliphAl-Hakim bi-Amr Allah ordered the destruction of all churches. In 1033, there was another earthquake, severely damaging the Al-Aqsa Mosque. The Fatimid caliph Ali az-Zahir rebuilt and completely renovated the mosque between 1034 and 1036. The number of naves was drastically reduced from fifteen to seven.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Jerusalem#cite_note-Nusseibeh-52) Az-Zahir built the four arcades of the central hall and aisle, which presently serve as the foundation of the mosque. The central aisle was double the width of the other aisles and had a large gable roof upon which the dome—made of wood—was constructed.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Jerusalem#cite_note-Elad-53) Persian geographer, Nasir Khusraw describes the Aqsa Mosque during a visit in 1047:
> The Haram Area (Noble Sanctuary) lies in the eastern part of the city; and through the bazaar of this (quarter) you enter the Area by a great and beautiful gateway (Dargah). ... After passing this gateway, you have on the right two great colonnades (Riwaq), each of which has nine-and-twenty marble pillars, whose capitals and bases are of colored marbles, and the joints are set in lead. Above the pillars rise arches, that are constructed, of masonry, without mortar or cement, and each arch is constructed of no more than five or six blocks of stone. These colonnades lead down to near the Maqsurah.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Jerusalem#cite_note-54)

## Medieval period
### Early Muslim period
#### Seljuk period
Under Az-Zahir's successor al-Mustansir Billah, the Fatimid Caliphate entered a period of instability and decline, as factions fought for power in Cairo. In 1071, Jerusalem was captured by the Turkish warlord Atsiz ibn Uvaq, who seized most of Syria and Palestine as part of the expansion of the Seljuk Turks throughout the Middle East. As the Turks were staunch Sunnis, they were opposed not only to the Fatimids, but also to the numerous Shia Muslims, who saw themselves removed from dominance after a century of Fatimid rule. In 1176, riots between Sunnis and Shiites in Jerusalem led to a massacre of the latter. Although the Christians of the city were left unmolested, and allowed access to the Christian holy sites, the wars with Byzantium and the general instability in Syria impeded the arrival pilgrims from Europe. The Seljuks also forbade the repair of any church, despite the damages suffered in the recent turmoils. There does not appear to have been a significant Jewish community in the city at this time.
In 1086, the Seljuk emir of Damascus, Tutush I, appointed Artuk Bey governor of Jerusalem. Artuk died in 1091, and his sons Sökmen and Ilghazi succeeded him. In August 1098, while the Seljuks were distracted by the arrival of the First Crusade in Syria, the Fatimids under vizier al-Afdal Shahanshah appeared before the city and laid siege to it. After six weeks, the Seljuk garrison capitulated and was allowed to leave for Damascus and Diyar Bakr. The Fatimid takeover was followed by the expulsion of most of the Sunnis, in which many of them were also killed.

## Medieval period
### Crusader/Ayyubid period
The time span consisting of the 12th and 13th centuries is sometimes referred to as the medieval period, or the Middle Ages, in the history of Jerusalem.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Jerusalem#cite_note-SWB2011-55)

## Three centuries that turned Jerusalem, Bethlehem, and Galilee into a Christian landscape
Constantine funded two churches. Helena identified two sites. What grew out of that beginning, across the following three centuries, was something on an entirely different scale: city walls paid for by an empress in exile, one of the largest basilicas in the Christian world raised on Justinian's orders, a Judean desert filling with hermits and monasteries, and pilgrims arriving from Gaul and Spain and Egypt in numbers large enough to require purpose-built hospices along the road.
Our companion article on **Constantine, Helena, and the transformation of Christianity** covers the founding moment; this article covers everything that followed — the period historians call Byzantine, running from the early fourth century until the region passed out of Christian imperial control in the seventh century.
It is the era that gave Jerusalem, Bethlehem, Galilee, and the Judean Desert much of the sacred architecture, monastic culture, and pilgrimage geography that still shape how Christians experience the **Holy Land**today. Some of its greatest buildings disappeared. Others were rebuilt repeatedly. A few institutions survived in astonishing continuity. Together they created a Christian landscape whose outlines remained visible long after Byzantine political rule itself had vanished.

## Three centuries that turned Jerusalem, Bethlehem, and Galilee into a Christian landscape
### What "Byzantine" Means for the Holy Land
"Byzantine" is a modern historians' label, not a term the people of the period used for themselves; they called their empire Roman, and it remained the eastern continuation of the Roman Empire long after imperial government disappeared in the West. For the Holy Land, the Byzantine period runs conventionally from Constantine's reign through the region's loss to the Muslim conquest in the seventh century — roughly three hundred years during which an empire that had once periodically persecuted Christians increasingly identified itself with Christianity.
A major step came in 380 under Emperor Theodosius I, when the Edict of Thessalonica gave imperial endorsement to the Nicene form of Christianity. It went significantly beyond Constantine's earlier policy of toleration, although the establishment of Nicene Christianity as the dominant imperial orthodoxy was a process rather than something completed by a single decree. The theological background reached back to the **Council of Nicaea in 325**, whose confession concerning Christ became a defining reference point in the doctrinal struggles of the fourth century.
What followed was not a single sustained building boom but successive waves of imperial and private patronage, monastic expansion, pilgrimage development, and local Christian institution-building, punctuated by real crises — plague, religious conflict, revolt, and eventually invasion — that this article does not smooth over. The Holy Land was becoming more visibly Christian, but that transformation took place within a religiously diverse population and was neither peaceful nor uncontested at every stage.
The Christian landscape of the Byzantine period was the result of a much longer story that had begun centuries earlier in Jerusalem. Our guide to **how Christianity began in Jerusalem and developed into the early Church** traces that foundation, before imperial patronage, monumental churches, and organized pilgrimage transformed the Holy Land so dramatically.
↑ Back to top

## Three centuries that turned Jerusalem, Bethlehem, and Galilee into a Christian landscape
### Empress Eudocia and the Walls of a Christian City
Aelia Eudocia, wife of the eastern emperor Theodosius II, first visited Jerusalem on pilgrimage in 438 and returned permanently around 443, after a falling-out with her husband's court that historians still debate the exact cause of. Whatever drove her there, she spent the final years of her life, until her death in 460, as one of Jerusalem's most significant patrons. She funded major building and charitable projects associated with the city's expanding Christian life, including new fortifications, a basilica honoring Saint Stephen, the Church's first martyr, and institutions serving the poor and the growing stream of pilgrims.
Eudocia's Jerusalem matters for a reason beyond any single building: she represents a shift from the emperor's-mother pilgrimage that Helena had modeled a century earlier toward something more permanent — an imperial figure who did not simply visit and depart, but relocated her life to the city and spent years embedding Christian institutions into its physical fabric.
The result belonged to a much broader change in **Jerusalem's development as Christianity's sacred city**. The Jerusalem encountered by fourth-century pilgrims had already been transformed by Constantine's churches. By Eudocia's lifetime, pilgrimage, charitable institutions, monastic communities, relic cults, liturgical processions, and imperial patronage were turning the city into something more elaborate: not simply a place containing Christian holy sites, but an urban landscape increasingly organized around Christian sacred memory.
↑ Back to top

## Three centuries that turned Jerusalem, Bethlehem, and Galilee into a Christian landscape
### Justinian's Jerusalem: The Nea Church and an Empire's Ambition
A century after Eudocia, Emperor Justinian brought a different kind of ambition to Jerusalem — the same instinct for monumental building he applied to Constantinople's Hagia Sophia. His Nea Church, formally the Church of the Theotokos, was consecrated in Jerusalem on November 20, 543, and by the account of Procopius, Justinian's own court historian, its construction required specially built roads and forty-ox teams to haul stone blocks and cedar timbers of extraordinary size from as far as Lebanon. It ranked among the largest church buildings anywhere in the Christian world at the time.
The Nea did not survive the centuries that followed, but twentieth-century excavations uncovered substantial remains, including massive foundation walls and a Greek dedicatory inscription explicitly naming Justinian. The discovery was unusually important because it allowed archaeology, literary description, and the surviving Byzantine representation of Jerusalem to illuminate one another.
Justinian's building program extended well beyond Jerusalem. He also rebuilt the **Church of the Nativity in Bethlehem** during the sixth century, replacing the earlier Constantinian basilica with the structure that forms the essential core of the church standing there today. The result is one of the most remarkable survivals of Byzantine Christian architecture anywhere in the Holy Land.
One further monument from this period deserves mention for what it tells historians rather than what it once looked like: the sixth-century mosaic floor map discovered in a church at Madaba, in modern Jordan. The **Madaba Map** depicts a wide sweep of the biblical lands, but its image of Jerusalem is especially detailed. The city appears from a kind of elevated perspective, with gates, streets, churches, and major monuments arranged so that a viewer standing over the mosaic could recognize the sacred geography of Byzantine Jerusalem.
Its representation of the city is not simply decorative. The great colonnaded street can be followed through the urban center; the Holy Sepulchre is prominently represented; and the Nea Church appears within the southern part of the city. For archaeologists, this sixth-century mosaic became something remarkably close to an ancient visual guide. When modern excavations uncovered the Nea's remains, the location shown on the Madaba Map helped make sense of the buried Byzantine city.

## Three centuries that turned Jerusalem, Bethlehem, and Galilee into a Christian landscape
### Justinian's Jerusalem: The Nea Church and an Empire's Ambition
The map also reveals how dramatically Christian priorities had reshaped Jerusalem's visual identity. A Roman city that had once been rebuilt as Aelia Capitolina was now being represented through its churches and Christian sacred places. The **Church of the Holy Sepulchre** occupies a conspicuous place in that image, reflecting the importance the Constantinian sanctuary had acquired at the heart of Christian Jerusalem. The Madaba mosaic is therefore more than an old map: it is a surviving picture of how Byzantine Christians imagined the Holy City itself.
↑ Back to top

## Three centuries that turned Jerusalem, Bethlehem, and Galilee into a Christian landscape
### Beyond Jerusalem: Bethlehem, Galilee, and a Christianized Landscape
Some sites preserve especially complicated layers of history. Magdala, Mount Tabor, Arbel, and Kursi each tell somewhat different stories about Jewish settlement, Christian pilgrimage, monastic life, and the later identification of biblical places. Our guide to **Magdala, Mount Tabor, Arbel, and Kursi** explores those sites individually. Seen together, however, they reveal the larger Byzantine pattern: the Christianization of the Holy Land was not the construction of one sacred capital in Jerusalem, but the gradual creation of an interconnected landscape extending from Judea through Bethlehem and north into Galilee.
↑ Back to top

## Three centuries that turned Jerusalem, Bethlehem, and Galilee into a Christian landscape
### Cracks in the Byzantine Peace: Revolt and the Persian Invasion
This was not, across three centuries, an uninterrupted story of peaceful construction. The Samaritan community of central Palestine, resentful of policies that increasingly restricted its position under a Christian empire, rose in a series of major revolts in the fifth and sixth centuries, including a particularly serious uprising in 529. The revolts were suppressed with considerable violence and contributed to a long-term decline in the Samaritan population. They are an important reminder that Byzantine Palestine's increasingly Christian public identity existed alongside Jewish, Samaritan, and other communities and could be imposed and contested rather than universally embraced.
The more decisive crisis came from outside the empire. In 614, Sasanian Persian forces captured Jerusalem during the great Byzantine-Sasanian war. Christian sources describe severe destruction and loss of life, although the precise scale and details remain subjects of historical and archaeological debate. Major Christian buildings were damaged, and the relic venerated in Jerusalem as the **True Cross** was carried away by the Persians.
Emperor Heraclius eventually reversed the war dramatically, forcing the Sasanian Empire into peace and recovering the relic. Its ceremonial restoration to Jerusalem at the end of the 620s or beginning of the 630s became one of the great symbolic moments of late Byzantine Christian memory. The episode further strengthened the association between Jerusalem, imperial power, and the Cross — an association whose much earlier origins are explored in our article on **Constantine and Saint Helena**.
The **Church of the Holy Sepulchre**, damaged during the Persian conquest, was repaired under the leadership traditionally associated with Modestus of Jerusalem. It would not be the last reconstruction. Fire, invasion, deliberate destruction, earthquakes, political changes, and competing Christian custodians would repeatedly alter the complex across the centuries, making the church standing today a physical record of Jerusalem's turbulent Christian history rather than a perfectly preserved fourth-century monument.
↑ Back to top

## Three centuries that turned Jerusalem, Bethlehem, and Galilee into a Christian landscape
### The End of Byzantine Jerusalem
Byzantine control had barely been restored after the Persian war when armies emerging from Arabia transformed the political map of the Near East. Byzantine forces suffered a decisive defeat at the Battle of Yarmouk in 636, after which Muslim armies consolidated control over much of Syria and Palestine. Jerusalem eventually negotiated terms of surrender, probably in **638**, although 637 also appears in traditional chronologies. Patriarch Sophronius was still leading Jerusalem's Christian community as Byzantine political authority in the city came to an end.
Later Christian and Muslim traditions connect Caliph Umar personally with Jerusalem's surrender and with guarantees protecting Christian lives, property, and places of worship. The exact wording and development of the various agreements associated with Umar are historically complex, and later documents should not simply be treated as verbatim transcripts of a single seventh-century treaty. What is clear is that Jerusalem passed into Muslim rule without experiencing the kind of destruction associated with the Persian capture of 614, and Christian institutions continued functioning under the new political order.
One famous later tradition tells that Patriarch Sophronius invited Umar to pray inside the **Church of the Holy Sepulchre** and that the caliph declined, fearing that later Muslims might use his prayer there as grounds to convert the church into a mosque. The story became an enduring part of Jerusalem's memory and appears in later historical accounts, but it should be understood as a tradition transmitted after the conquest rather than a securely documented eyewitness episode from 638. Medieval Muslim memory nevertheless associated Umar with the protection of Christian holy places in Jerusalem.
What changed decisively was political control, not the immediate disappearance of Christian Jerusalem. Churches continued to function. Pilgrims continued to arrive. Monasteries such as Mar Saba remained active. Local Christians had to learn how to live within a new Islamic political order, but the Christian sacred geography created during the Byzantine centuries survived the empire that had built so much of it. Scholarship on Palestine's transition from Byzantine to Islamic rule increasingly emphasizes this combination of political rupture and substantial local continuity.
↑ Back to top

## Three centuries that turned Jerusalem, Bethlehem, and Galilee into a Christian landscape
### What the Byzantine Holy Land Left Behind
The Byzantine centuries did not simply disappear when imperial rule ended; they left behind the physical and institutional skeleton that later Christian history in the Holy Land would keep building upon. The Church of the Nativity standing in Bethlehem today preserves the essential form of Justinian's sixth-century basilica. Mar Saba remains an active monastery rooted in the community Sabas founded some fifteen centuries ago. The Madaba Map still gives archaeologists an extraordinary image of the region's Christian topography. And beneath modern Jerusalem, Bethlehem, and Galilee, Byzantine walls, mosaics, foundations, cisterns, tombs, and inscriptions continue to emerge.
The period also helped shape forms of Eastern Christian life that survived the loss of Byzantine political control. Greek-speaking ecclesiastical traditions, monastic liturgy, the veneration of sacred places, and long-established Christian communities remained part of the region under successive rulers. That continuity forms an important part of the later history explored in our guide to the **Eastern Orthodox Church** and its relationship with the Holy Land.
Perhaps the most enduring Byzantine legacy, however, is less obvious than any individual building. These centuries helped establish the basic Christian map of the Holy Land. Jerusalem meant the Holy Sepulchre, the Mount of Olives, Gethsemane, and a sequence of places through which Christ's Passion could be remembered. Bethlehem centered Christian memory on the Nativity. Galilee became a landscape through which Gospel episodes could be followed from site to site. The Judean Desert became inseparable from monastic Christianity. Pilgrimage joined these places together.
The centuries after the Muslim conquest brought new rulers, new cultural worlds, periods of coexistence and conflict, and eventually the arrival of Latin Christian armies that captured Jerusalem in 1099. The **Crusades and the Holy Land** belong to a very different political and religious age. Yet the Jerusalem those armies fought over, and the Bethlehem and Galilee that later pilgrims sought, still rested heavily upon the sacred geography formed during the Byzantine centuries — by emperors and empresses, bishops and monks, craftsmen and donors, travelers like Egeria, and countless Christians whose names have disappeared while the places they helped shape remain.

#### What is meant by the "Byzantine Holy Land"?
It refers to the roughly three centuries, from the early fourth century to the Muslim conquest in the seventh century, when the Holy Land formed part of the Christian Roman Empire and Jerusalem, Bethlehem, Galilee, and the Judean Desert were extensively developed with churches, monasteries, and pilgrim infrastructure.

#### Who was Empress Eudocia and what did she build in Jerusalem?
Eudocia was a fifth-century Roman empress who eventually settled in Jerusalem. She became one of the city's major Christian patrons, associated with new fortifications, churches including a basilica honoring Saint Stephen, and charitable institutions serving the poor and pilgrims.

Those memories reached back to the beginnings of the faith. ## Three centuries that turned Jerusalem, Bethlehem, and Galilee into a Christian landscape
Constantine funded two churches. Helena identified two sites. What grew out of that beginning, across the following three centuries, was something on an entirely different scale: city walls paid for by an empress in exile, one of the largest basilicas in the Christian world raised on Justinian's orders, a Judean desert filling with hermits and monasteries, and pilgrims arriving from Gaul and Spain and Egypt in numbers large enough to require purpose-built hospices along the road.
Our companion article on **Constantine, Helena, and the transformation of Christianity** covers the founding moment; this article covers everything that followed — the period historians call Byzantine, running from the early fourth century until the region passed out of Christian imperial control in the seventh century.

## Three centuries that turned Jerusalem, Bethlehem, and Galilee into a Christian landscape
### What "Byzantine" Means for the Holy Land
"Byzantine" is a modern historians' label, not a term the people of the period used for themselves; they called their empire Roman, and it remained the eastern continuation of the Roman Empire long after imperial government disappeared in the West. For the Holy Land, the Byzantine period runs conventionally from Constantine's reign through the region's loss to the Muslim conquest in the seventh century — roughly three hundred years during which an empire that had once periodically persecuted Christians increasingly identified itself with Christianity.
A major step came in 380 under Emperor Theodosius I, when the Edict of Thessalonica gave imperial endorsement to the Nicene form of Christianity. It went significantly beyond Constantine's earlier policy of toleration, although the establishment of Nicene Christianity as the dominant imperial orthodoxy was a process rather than something completed by a single decree. The theological background reached back to the **Council of Nicaea in 325**, whose confession concerning Christ became a defining reference point in the doctrinal struggles of the fourth century.
What followed was not a single sustained building boom but successive waves of imperial and private patronage, monastic expansion, pilgrimage development, and local Christian institution-building, punctuated by real crises — plague, religious conflict, revolt, and eventually invasion — that this article does not smooth over. The Holy Land was becoming more visibly Christian, but that transformation took place within a religiously diverse population and was neither peaceful nor uncontested at every stage.
The Christian landscape of the Byzantine period was the result of a much longer story that had begun centuries earlier in Jerusalem. Our guide to **how Christianity began in Jerusalem and developed into the early Church** traces that foundation, before imperial patronage, monumental churches, and organized pilgrimage transformed the Holy Land so dramatically.
↑ Back to top

## Three centuries that turned Jerusalem, Bethlehem, and Galilee into a Christian landscape
### Empress Eudocia and the Walls of a Christian City
Aelia Eudocia, wife of the eastern emperor Theodosius II, first visited Jerusalem on pilgrimage in 438 and returned permanently around 443, after a falling-out with her husband's court that historians still debate the exact cause of. Whatever drove her there, she spent the final years of her life, until her death in 460, as one of Jerusalem's most significant patrons. She funded major building and charitable projects associated with the city's expanding Christian life, including new fortifications, a basilica honoring Saint Stephen, the Church's first martyr, and institutions serving the poor and the growing stream of pilgrims.
Eudocia's Jerusalem matters for a reason beyond any single building: she represents a shift from the emperor's-mother pilgrimage that Helena had modeled a century earlier toward something more permanent — an imperial figure who did not simply visit and depart, but relocated her life to the city and spent years embedding Christian institutions into its physical fabric.
The result belonged to a much broader change in **Jerusalem's development as Christianity's sacred city**. The Jerusalem encountered by fourth-century pilgrims had already been transformed by Constantine's churches. By Eudocia's lifetime, pilgrimage, charitable institutions, monastic communities, relic cults, liturgical processions, and imperial patronage were turning the city into something more elaborate: not simply a place containing Christian holy sites, but an urban landscape increasingly organized around Christian sacred memory.
↑ Back to top

## Three centuries that turned Jerusalem, Bethlehem, and Galilee into a Christian landscape
### Justinian's Jerusalem: The Nea Church and an Empire's Ambition
A century after Eudocia, Emperor Justinian brought a different kind of ambition to Jerusalem — the same instinct for monumental building he applied to Constantinople's Hagia Sophia. His Nea Church, formally the Church of the Theotokos, was consecrated in Jerusalem on November 20, 543, and by the account of Procopius, Justinian's own court historian, its construction required specially built roads and forty-ox teams to haul stone blocks and cedar timbers of extraordinary size from as far as Lebanon. It ranked among the largest church buildings anywhere in the Christian world at the time.
The Nea did not survive the centuries that followed, but twentieth-century excavations uncovered substantial remains, including massive foundation walls and a Greek dedicatory inscription explicitly naming Justinian. The discovery was unusually important because it allowed archaeology, literary description, and the surviving Byzantine representation of Jerusalem to illuminate one another.
Justinian's building program extended well beyond Jerusalem. He also rebuilt the **Church of the Nativity in Bethlehem** during the sixth century, replacing the earlier Constantinian basilica with the structure that forms the essential core of the church standing there today. The result is one of the most remarkable survivals of Byzantine Christian architecture anywhere in the Holy Land.
One further monument from this period deserves mention for what it tells historians rather than what it once looked like: the sixth-century mosaic floor map discovered in a church at Madaba, in modern Jordan. The **Madaba Map** depicts a wide sweep of the biblical lands, but its image of Jerusalem is especially detailed. The city appears from a kind of elevated perspective, with gates, streets, churches, and major monuments arranged so that a viewer standing over the mosaic could recognize the sacred geography of Byzantine Jerusalem.
Its representation of the city is not simply decorative. The great colonnaded street can be followed through the urban center; the Holy Sepulchre is prominently represented; and the Nea Church appears within the southern part of the city. For archaeologists, this sixth-century mosaic became something remarkably close to an ancient visual guide. When modern excavations uncovered the Nea's remains, the location shown on the Madaba Map helped make sense of the buried Byzantine city.

### Justinian's Jerusalem: The Nea Church and an Empire's Ambition
The map also reveals how dramatically Christian priorities had reshaped Jerusalem's visual identity. A Roman city that had once been rebuilt as Aelia Capitolina was now being represented through its churches and Christian sacred places. The **Church of the Holy Sepulchre** occupies a conspicuous place in that image, reflecting the importance the Constantinian sanctuary had acquired at the heart of Christian Jerusalem. The Madaba mosaic is therefore more than an old map: it is a surviving picture of how Byzantine Christians imagined the Holy City itself.

### Beyond Jerusalem: Bethlehem, Galilee, and a Christianized Landscape
Some sites preserve especially complicated layers of history. Magdala, Mount Tabor, Arbel, and Kursi each tell somewhat different stories about Jewish settlement, Christian pilgrimage, monastic life, and the later identification of biblical places. Our guide to **Magdala, Mount Tabor, Arbel, and Kursi** explores those sites individually. Seen together, however, they reveal the larger Byzantine pattern: the Christianization of the Holy Land was not the construction of one sacred capital in Jerusalem, but the gradual creation of an interconnected landscape extending from Judea through Bethlehem and north into Galilee.

## Three centuries that turned Jerusalem, Bethlehem, and Galilee into a Christian landscape
### Cracks in the Byzantine Peace: Revolt and the Persian Invasion
This was not, across three centuries, an uninterrupted story of peaceful construction. The Samaritan community of central Palestine, resentful of policies that increasingly restricted its position under a Christian empire, rose in a series of major revolts in the fifth and sixth centuries, including a particularly serious uprising in 529. The revolts were suppressed with considerable violence and contributed to a long-term decline in the Samaritan population. They are an important reminder that Byzantine Palestine's increasingly Christian public identity existed alongside Jewish, Samaritan, and other communities and could be imposed and contested rather than universally embraced.
The more decisive crisis came from outside the empire. In 614, Sasanian Persian forces captured Jerusalem during the great Byzantine-Sasanian war. Christian sources describe severe destruction and loss of life, although the precise scale and details remain subjects of historical and archaeological debate. Major Christian buildings were damaged, and the relic venerated in Jerusalem as the **True Cross** was carried away by the Persians.
Emperor Heraclius eventually reversed the war dramatically, forcing the Sasanian Empire into peace and recovering the relic. Its ceremonial restoration to Jerusalem at the end of the 620s or beginning of the 630s became one of the great symbolic moments of late Byzantine Christian memory. The episode further strengthened the association between Jerusalem, imperial power, and the Cross — an association whose much earlier origins are explored in our article on **Constantine and Saint Helena**.
The **Church of the Holy Sepulchre**, damaged during the Persian conquest, was repaired under the leadership traditionally associated with Modestus of Jerusalem. It would not be the last reconstruction. Fire, invasion, deliberate destruction, earthquakes, political changes, and competing Christian custodians would repeatedly alter the complex across the centuries, making the church standing today a physical record of Jerusalem's turbulent Christian history rather than a perfectly preserved fourth-century monument.
↑ Back to top

## Three centuries that turned Jerusalem, Bethlehem, and Galilee into a Christian landscape
### The End of Byzantine Jerusalem
Byzantine control had barely been restored after the Persian war when armies emerging from Arabia transformed the political map of the Near East. Byzantine forces suffered a decisive defeat at the Battle of Yarmouk in 636, after which Muslim armies consolidated control over much of Syria and Palestine. Jerusalem eventually negotiated terms of surrender, probably in **638**, although 637 also appears in traditional chronologies. Patriarch Sophronius was still leading Jerusalem's Christian community as Byzantine political authority in the city came to an end.
Later Christian and Muslim traditions connect Caliph Umar personally with Jerusalem's surrender and with guarantees protecting Christian lives, property, and places of worship. The exact wording and development of the various agreements associated with Umar are historically complex, and later documents should not simply be treated as verbatim transcripts of a single seventh-century treaty. What is clear is that Jerusalem passed into Muslim rule without experiencing the kind of destruction associated with the Persian capture of 614, and Christian institutions continued functioning under the new political order.
One famous later tradition tells that Patriarch Sophronius invited Umar to pray inside the **Church of the Holy Sepulchre** and that the caliph declined, fearing that later Muslims might use his prayer there as grounds to convert the church into a mosque. The story became an enduring part of Jerusalem's memory and appears in later historical accounts, but it should be understood as a tradition transmitted after the conquest rather than a securely documented eyewitness episode from 638. Medieval Muslim memory nevertheless associated Umar with the protection of Christian holy places in Jerusalem.
What changed decisively was political control, not the immediate disappearance of Christian Jerusalem. Churches continued to function. Pilgrims continued to arrive. Monasteries such as Mar Saba remained active. Local Christians had to learn how to live within a new Islamic political order, but the Christian sacred geography created during the Byzantine centuries survived the empire that had built so much of it. Scholarship on Palestine's transition from Byzantine to Islamic rule increasingly emphasizes this combination of political rupture and substantial local continuity.
↑ Back to top

## Three centuries that turned Jerusalem, Bethlehem, and Galilee into a Christian landscape
### What the Byzantine Holy Land Left Behind
The Byzantine centuries did not simply disappear when imperial rule ended; they left behind the physical and institutional skeleton that later Christian history in the Holy Land would keep building upon. The Church of the Nativity standing in Bethlehem today preserves the essential form of Justinian's sixth-century basilica. Mar Saba remains an active monastery rooted in the community Sabas founded some fifteen centuries ago. The Madaba Map still gives archaeologists an extraordinary image of the region's Christian topography. And beneath modern Jerusalem, Bethlehem, and Galilee, Byzantine walls, mosaics, foundations, cisterns, tombs, and inscriptions continue to emerge.
The period also helped shape forms of Eastern Christian life that survived the loss of Byzantine political control. Greek-speaking ecclesiastical traditions, monastic liturgy, the veneration of sacred places, and long-established Christian communities remained part of the region under successive rulers. That continuity forms an important part of the later history explored in our guide to the **Eastern Orthodox Church** and its relationship with the Holy Land.
Perhaps the most enduring Byzantine legacy, however, is less obvious than any individual building. These centuries helped establish the basic Christian map of the Holy Land. Jerusalem meant the Holy Sepulchre, the Mount of Olives, Gethsemane, and a sequence of places through which Christ's Passion could be remembered. Bethlehem centered Christian memory on the Nativity. Galilee became a landscape through which Gospel episodes could be followed from site to site. The Judean Desert became inseparable from monastic Christianity. Pilgrimage joined these places together.
The centuries after the Muslim conquest brought new rulers, new cultural worlds, periods of coexistence and conflict, and eventually the arrival of Latin Christian armies that captured Jerusalem in 1099. The **Crusades and the Holy Land** belong to a very different political and religious age. Yet the Jerusalem those armies fought over, and the Bethlehem and Galilee that later pilgrims sought, still rested heavily upon the sacred geography formed during the Byzantine centuries — by emperors and empresses, bishops and monks, craftsmen and donors, travelers like Egeria, and countless Christians whose names have disappeared while the places they helped shape remain.
↑ Back to top

## Late antiquity
### Byzantine period
In the Siege of Jerusalem of 614, after 21 days of relentless siege warfare, Jerusalem was captured. Byzantine chronicles relate that the Sassanids and Jews slaughtered tens of thousands of Christians in the city, many at the Mamilla Pool,[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Jerusalem#cite_note-43)[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Jerusalem#cite_note-44) and destroyed their monuments and churches, including the Church of the Holy Sepulchre. This episode has been the subject of much debate between historians.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Jerusalem#cite_note-45) Following the conquest, Jewish leaders briefly governed or held key roles in Jerusalem under Sassanid suzerainty (614–617 CE).[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Jerusalem#cite_note-46) In 617 AD, the Sassanid Empire reversed course and removed the Jewish control of the city. Jerusalem then stayed in Sassanid hands until the Byzantine emperor Heraclius reconquered it in 629.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Jerusalem#cite_note-47)

## Medieval period
### Early Muslim period
#### Rashidun, Umayyad and Abbasid Caliphates
Under the early centuries of Muslim rule, especially during the Umayyad (650–750) dynasty, the city prospered. Around 691–692 CE, the Dome of the Rock was built on the Temple Mount. Rather than a mosque, it is a shrine that enshrines the Foundation Stone. The Al-Aqsa Mosque was also built under Umayyad rule during the late 7th or early 8th century on the southern end of the compound, and was associated with a place of the same name mentioned in the Quran as a place visited by Muhammad during his [Night Journey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isra'_and_Mi'raj "Isra' and Mi'raj"). Jerusalem is not mentioned by any of its names in the Quran, and the Qur'an does not mention the exact location of Al-Aqsa Mosque.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Jerusalem#cite_note-Khatib-48)[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Jerusalem#cite_note-:9-49) Some scholars contend that the connection between the Al-Aqsa Mosque referenced in the Quran and the Temple Mount in Jerusalem is the result of an Umayyad political agenda that aimed to rival the prestige of the Mecca sanctuary, which was then ruled by their enemy, Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Jerusalem#cite_note-:8-50)[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Jerusalem#cite_note-51)
The Abbasid period (750–969) is the least documented of the early Muslim period in general. The Temple Mount area was the center of known building activity, with structures damaged in earthquakes being repaired.

## Medieval period
### Early Muslim period
#### Rashidun, Umayyad and Abbasid Caliphates
Geographers Ibn Hawqal and al-Istakhri (10th century) describe Jerusalem as "the most fertile province of Palestine",_[citation needed_] while its native son, the geographer al-Muqaddasi (born 946) devoted many pages to its praises in his most famous work, _The Best Divisions in the Knowledge of the Climes_. Under Muslim rule Jerusalem did not achieve the political or cultural status enjoyed by the capitals Damascus, Baghdad, Cairo etc. Al-Muqaddasi derives his name from the Arabic name for Jerusalem, _Bayt al-Muqaddas_, which is linguistically equivalent to the Hebrew _Beit Ha-Mikdash_, the Holy House.

### Early Muslim period
#### Fatimid period
The early Arab period was also one of religious tolerance._[citation needed_] However, in the early 11th century, the Egyptian Fatimid CaliphAl-Hakim bi-Amr Allah ordered the destruction of all churches. In 1033, there was another earthquake, severely damaging the Al-Aqsa Mosque. The Fatimid caliph Ali az-Zahir rebuilt and completely renovated the mosque between 1034 and 1036. The number of naves was drastically reduced from fifteen to seven.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Jerusalem#cite_note-Nusseibeh-52) Az-Zahir built the four arcades of the central hall and aisle, which presently serve as the foundation of the mosque. The central aisle was double the width of the other aisles and had a large gable roof upon which the dome—made of wood—was constructed.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Jerusalem#cite_note-Elad-53) Persian geographer, Nasir Khusraw describes the Aqsa Mosque during a visit in 1047:
> The Haram Area (Noble Sanctuary) lies in the eastern part of the city; and through the bazaar of this (quarter) you enter the Area by a great and beautiful gateway (Dargah). ... After passing this gateway, you have on the right two great colonnades (Riwaq), each of which has nine-and-twenty marble pillars, whose capitals and bases are of colored marbles, and the joints are set in lead. Above the pillars rise arches, that are constructed, of masonry, without mortar or cement, and each arch is constructed of no more than five or six blocks of stone. These colonnades lead down to near the Maqsurah.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Jerusalem#cite_note-54)

#### Seljuk period
Under Az-Zahir's successor al-Mustansir Billah, the Fatimid Caliphate entered a period of instability and decline, as factions fought for power in Cairo. In 1071, Jerusalem was captured by the Turkish warlord Atsiz ibn Uvaq, who seized most of Syria and Palestine as part of the expansion of the Seljuk Turks throughout the Middle East. As the Turks were staunch Sunnis, they were opposed not only to the Fatimids, but also to the numerous Shia Muslims, who saw themselves removed from dominance after a century of Fatimid rule. In 1176, riots between Sunnis and Shiites in Jerusalem led to a massacre of the latter. Although the Christians of the city were left unmolested, and allowed access to the Christian holy sites, the wars with Byzantium and the general instability in Syria impeded the arrival pilgrims from Europe. The Seljuks also forbade the repair of any church, despite the damages suffered in the recent turmoils. There does not appear to have been a significant Jewish community in the city at this time.
In 1086, the Seljuk emir of Damascus, Tutush I, appointed Artuk Bey governor of Jerusalem. Artuk died in 1091, and his sons Sökmen and Ilghazi succeeded him. In August 1098, while the Seljuks were distracted by the arrival of the First Crusade in Syria, the Fatimids under vizier al-Afdal Shahanshah appeared before the city and laid siege to it. After six weeks, the Seljuk garrison capitulated and was allowed to leave for Damascus and Diyar Bakr. The Fatimid takeover was followed by the expulsion of most of the Sunnis, in which many of them were also killed.

## Three centuries that turned Jerusalem, Bethlehem, and Galilee into a Christian landscape
Constantine funded two churches. Helena identified two sites. What grew out of that beginning, across the following three centuries, was something on an entirely different scale: city walls paid for by an empress in exile, one of the largest basilicas in the Christian world raised on Justinian's orders, a Judean desert filling with hermits and monasteries, and pilgrims arriving from Gaul and Spain and Egypt in numbers large enough to require purpose-built hospices along the road.
Our companion article on **Constantine, Helena, and the transformation of Christianity** covers the founding moment; this article covers everything that followed — the period historians call Byzantine, running from the early fourth century until the region passed out of Christian imperial control in the seventh century.
It is the era that gave Jerusalem, Bethlehem, Galilee, and the Judean Desert much of the sacred architecture, monastic culture, and pilgrimage geography that still shape how Christians experience the **Holy Land**today. Some of its greatest buildings disappeared. Others were rebuilt repeatedly. A few institutions survived in astonishing continuity. Together they created a Christian landscape whose outlines remained visible long after Byzantine political rule itself had vanished.

## Three centuries that turned Jerusalem, Bethlehem, and Galilee into a Christian landscape
### What "Byzantine" Means for the Holy Land
"Byzantine" is a modern historians' label, not a term the people of the period used for themselves; they called their empire Roman, and it remained the eastern continuation of the Roman Empire long after imperial government disappeared in the West. For the Holy Land, the Byzantine period runs conventionally from Constantine's reign through the region's loss to the Muslim conquest in the seventh century — roughly three hundred years during which an empire that had once periodically persecuted Christians increasingly identified itself with Christianity.
A major step came in 380 under Emperor Theodosius I, when the Edict of Thessalonica gave imperial endorsement to the Nicene form of Christianity. It went significantly beyond Constantine's earlier policy of toleration, although the establishment of Nicene Christianity as the dominant imperial orthodoxy was a process rather than something completed by a single decree. The theological background reached back to the **Council of Nicaea in 325**, whose confession concerning Christ became a defining reference point in the doctrinal struggles of the fourth century.
What followed was not a single sustained building boom but successive waves of imperial and private patronage, monastic expansion, pilgrimage development, and local Christian institution-building, punctuated by real crises — plague, religious conflict, revolt, and eventually invasion — that this article does not smooth over. The Holy Land was becoming more visibly Christian, but that transformation took place within a religiously diverse population and was neither peaceful nor uncontested at every stage.
The Christian landscape of the Byzantine period was the result of a much longer story that had begun centuries earlier in Jerusalem. Our guide to **how Christianity began in Jerusalem and developed into the early Church** traces that foundation, before imperial patronage, monumental churches, and organized pilgrimage transformed the Holy Land so dramatically.
↑ Back to top

## Three centuries that turned Jerusalem, Bethlehem, and Galilee into a Christian landscape
### Empress Eudocia and the Walls of a Christian City
Aelia Eudocia, wife of the eastern emperor Theodosius II, first visited Jerusalem on pilgrimage in 438 and returned permanently around 443, after a falling-out with her husband's court that historians still debate the exact cause of. Whatever drove her there, she spent the final years of her life, until her death in 460, as one of Jerusalem's most significant patrons. She funded major building and charitable projects associated with the city's expanding Christian life, including new fortifications, a basilica honoring Saint Stephen, the Church's first martyr, and institutions serving the poor and the growing stream of pilgrims.
Eudocia's Jerusalem matters for a reason beyond any single building: she represents a shift from the emperor's-mother pilgrimage that Helena had modeled a century earlier toward something more permanent — an imperial figure who did not simply visit and depart, but relocated her life to the city and spent years embedding Christian institutions into its physical fabric.
The result belonged to a much broader change in **Jerusalem's development as Christianity's sacred city**. The Jerusalem encountered by fourth-century pilgrims had already been transformed by Constantine's churches. By Eudocia's lifetime, pilgrimage, charitable institutions, monastic communities, relic cults, liturgical processions, and imperial patronage were turning the city into something more elaborate: not simply a place containing Christian holy sites, but an urban landscape increasingly organized around Christian sacred memory.
↑ Back to top

## Three centuries that turned Jerusalem, Bethlehem, and Galilee into a Christian landscape
### Justinian's Jerusalem: The Nea Church and an Empire's Ambition
A century after Eudocia, Emperor Justinian brought a different kind of ambition to Jerusalem — the same instinct for monumental building he applied to Constantinople's Hagia Sophia. His Nea Church, formally the Church of the Theotokos, was consecrated in Jerusalem on November 20, 543, and by the account of Procopius, Justinian's own court historian, its construction required specially built roads and forty-ox teams to haul stone blocks and cedar timbers of extraordinary size from as far as Lebanon. It ranked among the largest church buildings anywhere in the Christian world at the time.
The Nea did not survive the centuries that followed, but twentieth-century excavations uncovered substantial remains, including massive foundation walls and a Greek dedicatory inscription explicitly naming Justinian. The discovery was unusually important because it allowed archaeology, literary description, and the surviving Byzantine representation of Jerusalem to illuminate one another.
Justinian's building program extended well beyond Jerusalem. He also rebuilt the **Church of the Nativity in Bethlehem** during the sixth century, replacing the earlier Constantinian basilica with the structure that forms the essential core of the church standing there today. The result is one of the most remarkable survivals of Byzantine Christian architecture anywhere in the Holy Land.
One further monument from this period deserves mention for what it tells historians rather than what it once looked like: the sixth-century mosaic floor map discovered in a church at Madaba, in modern Jordan. The **Madaba Map** depicts a wide sweep of the biblical lands, but its image of Jerusalem is especially detailed. The city appears from a kind of elevated perspective, with gates, streets, churches, and major monuments arranged so that a viewer standing over the mosaic could recognize the sacred geography of Byzantine Jerusalem.
Its representation of the city is not simply decorative. The great colonnaded street can be followed through the urban center; the Holy Sepulchre is prominently represented; and the Nea Church appears within the southern part of the city. For archaeologists, this sixth-century mosaic became something remarkably close to an ancient visual guide. When modern excavations uncovered the Nea's remains, the location shown on the Madaba Map helped make sense of the buried Byzantine city.

## Three centuries that turned Jerusalem, Bethlehem, and Galilee into a Christian landscape
### Justinian's Jerusalem: The Nea Church and an Empire's Ambition
The map also reveals how dramatically Christian priorities had reshaped Jerusalem's visual identity. A Roman city that had once been rebuilt as Aelia Capitolina was now being represented through its churches and Christian sacred places. The **Church of the Holy Sepulchre** occupies a conspicuous place in that image, reflecting the importance the Constantinian sanctuary had acquired at the heart of Christian Jerusalem. The Madaba mosaic is therefore more than an old map: it is a surviving picture of how Byzantine Christians imagined the Holy City itself.
↑ Back to top

### Beyond Jerusalem: Bethlehem, Galilee, and a Christianized Landscape
Some sites preserve especially complicated layers of history. Magdala, Mount Tabor, Arbel, and Kursi each tell somewhat different stories about Jewish settlement, Christian pilgrimage, monastic life, and the later identification of biblical places. Our guide to **Magdala, Mount Tabor, Arbel, and Kursi** explores those sites individually. Seen together, however, they reveal the larger Byzantine pattern: the Christianization of the Holy Land was not the construction of one sacred capital in Jerusalem, but the gradual creation of an interconnected landscape extending from Judea through Bethlehem and north into Galilee.
↑ Back to top

## Three centuries that turned Jerusalem, Bethlehem, and Galilee into a Christian landscape
### Cracks in the Byzantine Peace: Revolt and the Persian Invasion
This was not, across three centuries, an uninterrupted story of peaceful construction. The Samaritan community of central Palestine, resentful of policies that increasingly restricted its position under a Christian empire, rose in a series of major revolts in the fifth and sixth centuries, including a particularly serious uprising in 529. The revolts were suppressed with considerable violence and contributed to a long-term decline in the Samaritan population. They are an important reminder that Byzantine Palestine's increasingly Christian public identity existed alongside Jewish, Samaritan, and other communities and could be imposed and contested rather than universally embraced.
The more decisive crisis came from outside the empire. In 614, Sasanian Persian forces captured Jerusalem during the great Byzantine-Sasanian war. Christian sources describe severe destruction and loss of life, although the precise scale and details remain subjects of historical and archaeological debate. Major Christian buildings were damaged, and the relic venerated in Jerusalem as the **True Cross** was carried away by the Persians.
Emperor Heraclius eventually reversed the war dramatically, forcing the Sasanian Empire into peace and recovering the relic. Its ceremonial restoration to Jerusalem at the end of the 620s or beginning of the 630s became one of the great symbolic moments of late Byzantine Christian memory. The episode further strengthened the association between Jerusalem, imperial power, and the Cross — an association whose much earlier origins are explored in our article on **Constantine and Saint Helena**.
The **Church of the Holy Sepulchre**, damaged during the Persian conquest, was repaired under the leadership traditionally associated with Modestus of Jerusalem. It would not be the last reconstruction. Fire, invasion, deliberate destruction, earthquakes, political changes, and competing Christian custodians would repeatedly alter the complex across the centuries, making the church standing today a physical record of Jerusalem's turbulent Christian history rather than a perfectly preserved fourth-century monument.
↑ Back to top

## Three centuries that turned Jerusalem, Bethlehem, and Galilee into a Christian landscape
### The End of Byzantine Jerusalem
Byzantine control had barely been restored after the Persian war when armies emerging from Arabia transformed the political map of the Near East. Byzantine forces suffered a decisive defeat at the Battle of Yarmouk in 636, after which Muslim armies consolidated control over much of Syria and Palestine. Jerusalem eventually negotiated terms of surrender, probably in **638**, although 637 also appears in traditional chronologies. Patriarch Sophronius was still leading Jerusalem's Christian community as Byzantine political authority in the city came to an end.
Later Christian and Muslim traditions connect Caliph Umar personally with Jerusalem's surrender and with guarantees protecting Christian lives, property, and places of worship. The exact wording and development of the various agreements associated with Umar are historically complex, and later documents should not simply be treated as verbatim transcripts of a single seventh-century treaty. What is clear is that Jerusalem passed into Muslim rule without experiencing the kind of destruction associated with the Persian capture of 614, and Christian institutions continued functioning under the new political order.
One famous later tradition tells that Patriarch Sophronius invited Umar to pray inside the **Church of the Holy Sepulchre** and that the caliph declined, fearing that later Muslims might use his prayer there as grounds to convert the church into a mosque. The story became an enduring part of Jerusalem's memory and appears in later historical accounts, but it should be understood as a tradition transmitted after the conquest rather than a securely documented eyewitness episode from 638. Medieval Muslim memory nevertheless associated Umar with the protection of Christian holy places in Jerusalem.
What changed decisively was political control, not the immediate disappearance of Christian Jerusalem. Churches continued to function. Pilgrims continued to arrive. Monasteries such as Mar Saba remained active. Local Christians had to learn how to live within a new Islamic political order, but the Christian sacred geography created during the Byzantine centuries survived the empire that had built so much of it. Scholarship on Palestine's transition from Byzantine to Islamic rule increasingly emphasizes this combination of political rupture and substantial local continuity.
↑ Back to top

## Three centuries that turned Jerusalem, Bethlehem, and Galilee into a Christian landscape
### What the Byzantine Holy Land Left Behind
The Byzantine centuries did not simply disappear when imperial rule ended; they left behind the physical and institutional skeleton that later Christian history in the Holy Land would keep building upon. The Church of the Nativity standing in Bethlehem today preserves the essential form of Justinian's sixth-century basilica. Mar Saba remains an active monastery rooted in the community Sabas founded some fifteen centuries ago. The Madaba Map still gives archaeologists an extraordinary image of the region's Christian topography. And beneath modern Jerusalem, Bethlehem, and Galilee, Byzantine walls, mosaics, foundations, cisterns, tombs, and inscriptions continue to emerge.
The period also helped shape forms of Eastern Christian life that survived the loss of Byzantine political control. Greek-speaking ecclesiastical traditions, monastic liturgy, the veneration of sacred places, and long-established Christian communities remained part of the region under successive rulers. That continuity forms an important part of the later history explored in our guide to the **Eastern Orthodox Church** and its relationship with the Holy Land.
Perhaps the most enduring Byzantine legacy, however, is less obvious than any individual building. These centuries helped establish the basic Christian map of the Holy Land. Jerusalem meant the Holy Sepulchre, the Mount of Olives, Gethsemane, and a sequence of places through which Christ's Passion could be remembered. Bethlehem centered Christian memory on the Nativity. Galilee became a landscape through which Gospel episodes could be followed from site to site. The Judean Desert became inseparable from monastic Christianity. Pilgrimage joined these places together.
The centuries after the Muslim conquest brought new rulers, new cultural worlds, periods of coexistence and conflict, and eventually the arrival of Latin Christian armies that captured Jerusalem in 1099. The **Crusades and the Holy Land** belong to a very different political and religious age. Yet the Jerusalem those armies fought over, and the Bethlehem and Galilee that later pilgrims sought, still rested heavily upon the sacred geography formed during the Byzantine centuries — by emperors and empresses, bishops and monks, craftsmen and donors, travelers like Egeria, and countless Christians whose names have disappeared while the places they helped shape remain.
↑ Back to top

### Frequently Asked Questions
#### What is meant by the "Byzantine Holy Land"?
It refers to the roughly three centuries, from the early fourth century to the Muslim conquest in the seventh century, when the Holy Land formed part of the Christian Roman Empire and Jerusalem, Bethlehem, Galilee, and the Judean Desert were extensively developed with churches, monasteries, and pilgrim infrastructure.

## Three centuries that turned Jerusalem, Bethlehem, and Galilee into a Christian landscape
### Frequently Asked Questions
#### Who was Empress Eudocia and what did she build in Jerusalem?
Eudocia was a fifth-century Roman empress who eventually settled in Jerusalem. She became one of the city's major Christian patrons, associated with new fortifications, churches including a basilica honoring Saint Stephen, and charitable institutions serving the poor and pilgrims.

## Three centuries that turned Jerusalem, Bethlehem, and Galilee into a Christian landscape
### Frequently Asked Questions
#### What was Justinian's Nea Church?
The Nea Church, consecrated in Jerusalem in 543, was an enormous basilica funded by Emperor Justinian. Procopius described its construction as a major engineering undertaking, and substantial remains of the church were uncovered by twentieth-century archaeologists.

## Three centuries that turned Jerusalem, Bethlehem, and Galilee into a Christian landscape
### Frequently Asked Questions
#### Why did so many monks settle in the Judean Desert?
Beginning in the fourth century, ascetics such as Chariton, Euthymius, and later Sabas were drawn to the desert's isolation as a place for prayer and solitude close to Jerusalem's holy sites. Their communities developed into an extensive monastic landscape that included Mar Saba.

## Three centuries that turned Jerusalem, Bethlehem, and Galilee into a Christian landscape
### Frequently Asked Questions

Sasanian Persian forces captured Jerusalem in 614, and many Christian buildings were damaged or destroyed. The relic venerated as the True Cross was carried away. Byzantine forces later recovered the relic, which was ceremonially restored to Jerusalem during the reign of Emperor Heraclius.

### Frequently Asked Questions

Jerusalem negotiated terms of surrender during the Muslim conquest, probably in 638. Christian communities, churches, monasteries, and pilgrimage continued under Muslim rule, although the political framework of the Holy Land had fundamentally changed.

## Three centuries that turned Jerusalem, Bethlehem, and Galilee into a Christian landscape
### Closing Reflection
What strikes anyone who spends time with this period is how much of it survives by accident as much as design. An empress's exile becomes a chapter in Jerusalem's walls. A court historian's boast about ox-teams becomes a rare written witness to a church otherwise reduced to foundation stones. A traveler's reports to distant Christian women become the clearest window historians have into how Jerusalem prayed sixteen centuries ago. A mosaic floor in Jordan preserves a map of a city whose Byzantine streets and monuments would otherwise be far harder to reconstruct.
And then there is Mar Saba. Monks still descend the same desert gorge where Sabas established his community in the fifth century, long after the emperors who ruled the Holy Land disappeared. Bethlehem's great basilica still rises above the traditional place of Christ's birth. Christians still gather at the Holy Sepulchre. Pilgrims still move between Jerusalem, Bethlehem, the Mount of Olives, and Galilee, following a sacred geography that Byzantine Christians helped give physical form.
Empires rise in this story and empires fall — Roman rule becomes Christian Roman rule, Jerusalem falls to Persia and returns to Byzantium, and Byzantine authority finally gives way to Muslim government. Yet the churches, desert cells, pilgrim roads, mosaics, liturgies, and memories outlasted the political world that created them.
That may be the Byzantine Holy Land's most enduring legacy. It did not create Christianity's attachment to Jerusalem, Bethlehem, or Galilee. Those memories reached back to the beginnings of the faith. What the Byzantine centuries did was give those memories architecture, roads, monasteries, processions, mosaics, institutions, and a landscape through which Christians could physically walk.
Much of that landscape is still there.
